articles.title: BepiColombo’s Mercury arrival begins - full replay
articles.description:
Video: 
			02:31:10
				
Watch the replay of the livestream originally broadcast on 3 September as ESA/JAXA's BepiColombo mission took the first critical step towards arriving at Mercury.
After travelling through the inner Solar System together for eight years, BepiColombo's Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) will separate from the rest of the stacked spacecraft on 3 September 2026. This marks the beginning of one of the most complex planetary arrival sequences ever attempted by ESA.
Broadcast live from ESA's European Space Operations Centre (ESOC) in Darmstadt, Germany, the programme includes live views from the iconic Main Control Room, expert analysis, behind-the-scenes insights, and the first signal from the spacecraft following separation. 
Livestream schedule (CEST): 

13:45 – Livestream begins 
16:00-16:45 – End of livestream
articles.summary: BepiColombo successfully arrived at Mercury, marking a historic milestone in planetary exploration by the ESA and JAXA. The mission's livestream replay documents this extraordinary achievement in real-time.

articles.title: SpaceX launches 4 astronauts on a fast track to the International Space Station
articles.description: Four astronauts rocketed into orbit Thursday on a space station mission that will stretch until spring, among them a Canadian whose wife will give birth while he's away.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: SpaceX successfully launched four astronauts to the International Space Station on an accelerated trajectory. The crew will conduct research aboard the ISS through spring in this landmark human spaceflight mission.

articles.title: A record-breaking X-ray flash may reveal the birth of a magnetar
articles.description: Astronomers have found strong evidence that some mysterious, minutes-long X-ray flashes are produced when two neutron stars collide and create a magnetar. One record-setting event glowed in X-rays for nearly 10 minutes, potentially opening a new way to find these extreme cosmic mergers.
articles.summary: Astronomers have discovered evidence that mysterious X-ray flashes represent the birth of magnetars from colliding neutron stars. This landmark finding solves a long-standing astronomical puzzle.

articles.title: NASA's Perseverance Mars rover finds groundwater, lakes, and hot fluids in one place
articles.description: NASA’s Perseverance rover has uncovered a surprisingly complicated history of water in Jezero Crater. Scientists expected the crater’s Margin Unit to contain lake sediments, but instead found ancient igneous rocks that were altered by water on at least three separate occasions.
articles.summary: NASA's Perseverance rover has made a groundbreaking discovery of groundwater, ancient lakes, and hydrothermal systems in Jezero Crater. These findings reveal Mars had complex water chemistry that may have supported microbial life.

articles.title: The Universe Is Full of Tiny Red Dots—and They’re One of Astronomy’s Biggest Discoveries in Decades
articles.description: A new type of object found in the early universe has puzzled astronomers for years, but they may finally have some answers.
articles.summary: Astronomers have identified a new type of mysterious object in the early universe known as 'tiny red dots,' representing one of the biggest astronomical discoveries in decades. These enigmatic objects are rewriting our understanding of early galactic formation.

articles.title: La señal de la Voyager 1 ya tarda casi un día en llegar: la nave está a 25.700 millones de km y a punto de hacer historia
articles.description: El 13 de noviembre se convertirá en el primer objeto humano a un día luz de la Tierra. La NASA apaga instrumentos para mantenerla con vida
articles.summary: Voyager 1 approaches a historic milestone, becoming the first human-made object to reach one light-day distance from Earth at 25.7 billion kilometers, showcasing humanity's greatest deep space achievement.

articles.title: Avec 52 tonnes en orbite lors de son 14e vol, Starship entre dans le top 3 des plus gros lanceurs de l’histoire
articles.description: SpaceX a placé 26 satellites Starlink V3 en orbite ce lundi 28 septembre 2026, lors du 14e vol de son Starship. Ils pèsent environ 52 tonnes au total. Une infographie publiée sur X classe ce chargement au troisième rang des plus lourds de l'histoire, derrière…
articles.summary: SpaceX's Starship completes its 14th flight with 52 tonnes in orbit, entering the top 3 most powerful launch vehicles in history and deploying 26 Starlink V3 satellites.

articles.title: Science begins for Smile
articles.description: On 23 September, the European-Chinese Smile mission was declared ready to start revealing how Earth responds to the wind of charged particles from the Sun. This follows a busy in-space commissioning period since the spacecraft launched on 19 May and reached its target orbit for science operations on 20 June.
articles.summary: The European-Chinese Smile mission has been declared ready to begin science operations, studying how Earth's magnetosphere responds to solar wind. This collaborative mission opens new insights into our planet's interaction with space.

articles.title: Galaxies in a cosmic house of mirrors
articles.description:
Image:
			
This NASA/ESA/CSA James Webb Space Telescope Picture of the Month features galaxies in great detail that have been warped and multiplied like they’ve stepped into a house of mirrors. The brilliant golden galaxies splashed across this image belong to a galaxy cluster called MACS J0454.1-0300. The orange galaxies concentrated on one side of the cluster are not actually part of the cluster and are much farther away from us.
MACS J0454.1-0300 is itself immensely distant: the light from these galaxies has been travelling to us for so long that we’re seeing the cluster as it was when the Universe was about 8 billion years old. While this galaxy cluster is a valuable scientific target in its own right, the real stars of this image are the galaxies that appear warped and stretched, like a painting that has been smeared by a giant hand.
The way these galaxies look is the result of gravitational lensing, in which the enormous mass of a foreground object such as a galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light from a more distant object in the background. Gravitational lensing allows astronomers to observe galaxies, star clusters and even individual stars that are too far away for our telescopes to see under normal conditions. While the large, orange galaxies appear obviously distorted, look carefully at some of the small reddish background galaxies throughout this picture: even at the very edges of the frame, there are galaxies whose images have been bent into tiny arcs by MACS J0454.1-0300’s gravity.
The gravitationally lensed areas show multiple images of galaxies from when the Universe was young: a group of galaxies 2 billion years after the Big Bang, and a single galaxy just 800 million years old after the Big Bang. The galaxy group appears to be going through a merger, resulting in an enormous burst of star formation.
Astronomers have also identified individual bright ‘knots’ within the gravitationally lensed areas, corresponding to regions as small as 5 light-years across. These tiny clumps appear magnified by a factor of more than 300, in some cases.
A NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image of this same cluster was released in 2014. Take a moment to compare the two images; the difference between them is dramatic. The new Webb image reveals hundreds of galaxies missing from the earlier image. These galaxies were there all along, but Webb is much more sensitive to their much redder light.
The data behind this image come from two observing programmes (#5058, PI: Furtak; #6882, PI: Fujimoto) that leverage the ability of massive galaxy clusters to bring distant objects into view.
[Image Description: A massive galaxy cluster, made of many golden elliptical galaxies with the largest, brightest one in the centre. Heavily distorted orange galaxies appear all around the cluster, the largest concentrated in a large arc around the cluster's centre; these are images of very distant galaxies, created by gravitational lensing. A few galaxies are large and bluish-white in colour; bright, nearby stars are the same colour.]
Release on esawebb.org
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope reveals galaxies in unprecedented detail through a natural gravitational lensing effect. This spectacular image showcases the universe's hidden cosmic structures magnified across space.

articles.title: First Direct Image of Protoplanet Swirling Surrounding Gas
articles.description: The formation and evolution of planets is the driving force behind both where and how we might find life beyond Earth. This complex and lengthy process first begins with a massive ball of gas and dust that swirls until it flattens into a disk, followed by rocks ranging in size from pebbles to kilometer-scale objects clumping together in a process known as accretion, as they too swirl around within the larger disk and form rocky planets closer to the star and the farther out planets collect the gas, ice, and dust that the star couldn’t evaporate. Until now, researchers have been limited to visualizing the swirling gas and dust forming planets through computer models.
articles.summary: Astronomers have captured the first direct image of a protoplanet surrounded by swirling gas, revealing planetary formation in action. This breakthrough provides unprecedented insight into how planets are born.

articles.title: Coldest Lava Exoplanet Found to Hold an Atmosphere
articles.description: Exoplanets continue to challenge our understanding of planetary formation, evolution, and whether they might be able to support life as we know it. Scientists often use planets in our solar system as analogs for exoplanets, studying exoplanets with extremely short orbital periods forces scientists to constantly rethink our understanding of what planets can withstand during their lifetimes. One such type of exoplanet that has entered the foray in recent years are “lava world” exoplanets, and especially lava exoplanets that orbit dangerously close to their stars. But while it has been long known that lava worlds on with higher temperatures have atmospheres, “colder” lava worlds have been found to lack atmospheres.
articles.summary: Researchers have discovered an unusually cool lava exoplanet that retains an atmosphere, challenging previous formation theories. This unexpected find expands the diversity of exoplanet characteristics.

articles.title: Finding Life on Enceladus Could be Easier than We Thought, Says New Research
articles.description: Planetary scientists from Freie Universität Berlin have published two new studies that indicate that a spacecraft could identify evidence of life much more easily than previously thought.
articles.summary: New research from Freie Universität Berlin suggests that detecting life on Saturn's moon Enceladus may be easier than previously thought. This discovery enhances the prospects for finding extraterrestrial life in our solar system.

articles.title: The Rate of Starbirth is Crashing in the "Modern" Universe
articles.description: The Universe has been making fewer stars lately and astronomers want to know why. The obvious answer is: there hasn't been enough starbirth material. But, is that true? Is some other process at play? An international team led by researcher Hong Guo of the Chinese Academy of Sciences decided to dig into the reasons why it looks like starbirth is falling off.
articles.summary: Astronomers are investigating why the universe has dramatically slowed its rate of star formation in recent cosmic history. This discovery offers insights into the evolving processes that shape galaxy development across billions of years.

articles.title: Following ancient rain toward life-related chemistry clues on Mars
articles.description: The Mars we know today is a cold, dry world of dust and rocks. However, around 3.8–3.6 billion years ago, it may have looked very different. Geological and mineral evidence suggests that, in its distant past, the planet experienced periods warm and wet enough for water to exist on its surface, potentially forming rivers, lakes and even an ocean in the northern hemisphere.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Scientists are using ancient Martian water signatures to understand the chemical conditions that may have supported life billions of years ago. This research brings us closer to understanding Mars' potentially habitable past.

articles.title: A cleaner X-ray view of our galactic center's hot mess
articles.description: The center of the Milky Way galaxy is a chaotic place. In addition to the 4-million-solar-mass black hole known as Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the region is full of gas, dust, strong magnetic fields and stars in various stages of life—from birth to death.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Advanced X-ray observations reveal intricate details about the environment surrounding Sagittarius A*, the supermassive black hole at our galaxy's center. These clearer images enhance our understanding of extreme cosmic physics.

articles.title: Stratospheric observatory Sunrise-III reveals intricate solar magnetic structures
articles.description: A team of researchers led by the National Astronomical Observatory of Japan discovered unexpectedly intricate magnetic structures above quiet-sun regions by observing the sun with the balloon-borne solar observatory Sunrise-III during its 2024 flight in Earth's stratosphere. The work is published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: The Sunrise-III stratospheric observatory has revealed surprising complexity in the Sun's magnetic field structures. These detailed observations advance our understanding of solar physics and magnetic dynamics.

articles.title: Astronomers link mysterious cosmic flashes to collisions of dead stars
articles.description: For decades, astronomers have identified collisions between two neutron stars through bursts of gamma rays that can disappear in less than two seconds. But some of these violent encounters may also reveal themselves through X-ray flashes lasting several minutes. A new study published in Science Bulletin provides evidence for this connection, suggesting that merging neutron stars could be hiding among cosmic flashes whose origins have remained uncertain.
articles.source: Space News - Space, Astronomy, Space Exploration
articles.summary: Astronomers have identified the source of mysterious cosmic flashes as collisions between neutron stars. This breakthrough connects years of observations to a clear physical phenomenon.

articles.title: Watch Live: NASA’s Crew-13 could make the fastest U.S. trip to the ISS ever
articles.description: NASA’s SpaceX Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1. The Dragon could reach the orbiting laboratory in just 7 hours and 50 minutes, making it the fastest U.S. spacecraft journey to the ISS in history.
articles.summary: NASA's Crew-13 mission is scheduled to launch astronauts to the ISS on October 1, potentially achieving the fastest U.S. crewed journey to the station. This demonstrates advancing capabilities in rapid space access.

articles.title: The ice blasting from Saturn's moon Enceladus is stranger than scientists realized
articles.description: Enceladus may naturally separate and concentrate chemicals from its hidden ocean as droplets slowly freeze and shatter on their way into space. The process could explain Cassini’s puzzling ice-grain chemistry while giving future spacecraft a powerful advantage in searching for organic compounds and clues to life.
articles.summary: New research reveals that Saturn's moon Enceladus has a remarkable natural process that concentrates organic chemicals from its subsurface ocean. This discovery enhances our understanding of this potentially habitable ocean world.

articles.title: NASA’s Curiosity rover just hit 5,000 days on Mars and sent back this stunning view
articles.description: NASA’s Curiosity rover marked 5,000 Martian days by capturing morning and afternoon views that were blended into a striking Mars “postcard.” The panorama shows Curiosity, its tracks, and the enormous landscape surrounding Mount Sharp and Gale Crater.
articles.summary: NASA's Curiosity rover celebrated 5,000 Martian days of exploration by capturing stunning panoramic views of the Martian landscape. This milestone demonstrates the rover's enduring capability and scientific value.

articles.title: NASA’s Crew-13 could go from Florida to the ISS in under 9 hours
articles.description: NASA and SpaceX could launch four astronauts to the International Space Station on October 1, with the Dragon spacecraft reaching orbiting outpost less than nine hours after liftoff. Crew-13 will join Expedition 75 after teams complete a final round of intensive launch-readiness checks.
articles.summary: NASA and SpaceX are prepared to launch four astronauts to the ISS in under nine hours, achieving unprecedented speed for crewed spaceflight. This accomplishment represents a major advancement in rapid space access capabilities.

articles.title: Black hole jets may decide the fate of entire galaxies
articles.description: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas far beyond a galaxy’s visible edge, leaving a glowing trail hundreds of thousands of light-years long. By keeping this gas hot and preventing it from falling inward, the jets may help determine whether a galaxy keeps forming stars or becomes quiet.
articles.summary: Powerful jets from supermassive black holes can disturb star-forming gas across vast cosmic distances, influencing the fate of entire galaxies. This discovery reveals how black holes play a critical role in galaxy evolution and development.

articles.title: Is the universe infinite? The answer gets weird fast
articles.description: Measurements of ancient light from the cosmic microwave background suggest that the universe is remarkably flat. But that does not prove it is infinite, because the observable cosmos could be only a small patch of a much larger curved universe. Space could even be flat while wrapping around on itself in exotic ways.
articles.summary: Measurements of the cosmic microwave background suggest the universe is remarkably flat, with profound implications for understanding the universe's geometry and structure. This finding deepens our understanding of fundamental cosmic properties.

articles.title: China's FAST telescope to advance with Phase II construction as project marks 10th anniversary
articles.description: The Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST), known as the China's "Sky Eyes", will mark the 10th anniversary of its inauguration on September 25. Since its launch, the facility has achieved a series of landmark scientific and technologica…
articles.summary: China's FAST telescope, the world's largest single-dish radio telescope, advances to Phase II construction as it marks its 10th anniversary as a transformative astronomical instrument. This expansion will enhance humanity's ability to probe the cosmos.

articles.title: Crew-13 Mission [planned for October 1, 2026]
articles.description: SpaceX and NASA are targeting Thursday, October 1 for Falcon 9's launch of Dragon's 13th operational human spaceflight mission (Crew-13) to the International Space Station from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida.…
articles.summary: NASA and SpaceX prepare for the Crew-13 Dragon mission launching October 1, 2026, continuing the critical human spaceflight partnership to the ISS.

articles.title: ARTEMIS II-BESATZUNG ERHÄLT DIE STEPHEN HAWKING MEDAL
articles.description: Die Astronauten Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch und Jeremy Hansen wurden dafür geehrt, dass sie durch ihre herausragende Vermittlung der Wissenschaft, der Technik und des menschlichen Abenteuers im Rahmen von Artemis II Millionen von Menschen insp…
articles.summary: The Artemis II crew—Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen—receives the Stephen Hawking Medal for advancing human space exploration.

articles.title: Starship’s first orbital flight put its heat shield to the test – how it fares could determine if SpaceX’s vision is possible
articles.description: Starship’s heat shield is made of up of an array of ceramic tiles. Each is a small component, but together they have large consequences.
articles.summary: Starship's ceramic heat shield successfully withstands orbital reentry testing, validating critical technology for SpaceX's long-term space exploration vision.

articles.title: SpaceX Wins Analysts Praise, Buy Ratings After Starship Flight 14
articles.description: SpaceX stock rose early Tuesday as analysts praised the milestone Starship flight 14 mission executed by Elon Musk's rocket company on Monday. The launch marked the first orbital and revenue-generating flight for the Starship, as SpaceX pushes toward rocket r…
articles.summary: SpaceX receives analyst praise and buy ratings following the successful Starship Flight 14 milestone mission, demonstrating technological progress.

articles.title: Alien life? Why the possibility of exoplanet LHS 1140b emitting helium gas is so exciting
articles.description: The exoplanet LHS 1140b may have a temperature that could allow for liquid water on its surface. Just possibly, it could support the existence of life.
articles.summary: Exoplanet LHS 1140b shows potential signs of helium gas emissions and conditions for liquid water, sparking exciting possibilities for habitability and biosignatures.

articles.title: Something Massive Is Hiding in the Kuiper Belt (And It's Not Planet 9) [20:26]
articles.description: The map of our solar system has changed. For most of history, we viewed our neighborhood as a tidy, organized place. We thought it was a simple system with eight planets orbiting a star, surrounded by a clean void. We assumed there was a clear finish line whe…
articles.summary: New discoveries in the Kuiper Belt reveal massive hidden objects reshaping our understanding of the solar system's outer regions and planetary formation.
